The Atlanta Fed’s Q4 real GDP tracker though eased to +3.38%, the least since its +3.22% initiation on October 29th, down from +3.48% on November 9th.

The biggest move since the last update was a -0.15% drop in the contribution from residential investment (to -0.12% from +0.03%), mostly after last Wednesday’s existing home sales report. 

Consumption's contribution also fell -0.07% (to +1.72% from +1.79%), mostly after today’s reports (which looks strange given the strength of the control group, but the model actually raised its goods spending estimate; the drag came from services, led by a plunge in October utility spending in today’s industrial production data and a drop in restaurant sales; also September retail spending was revised up giving a higher compare). Those were partly offset by gains in inventories (+0.09%) and government spending (+0.06%).

As a reminder, the Atlanta Fed’s tracker started very strong in each of Q1, Q2 and Q3 before falling sharply as we approached the actual GDP reads: Q1 went from 3.13% to 1.99%, Q2 from 3.70% to 1.50%, and Q3 from 4.95% to 3.37%. We're far from that point, though, as we won't get the Q4 report until late January.

The reading for now remains well above the blue chip consensus* of ~+2.1%.

Here’s the breakdown of the components as of November 17th and changes from my last update November 9th:

Consumption = +1.72% (-0.07%)

Nonresidential fixed investment (biz spending) = +1.35% (-0.04%)

Inventories = +0.61% (+0.09%)

Gov’t = +0.27% (+0.06%)

Residential investment = -0.12% (-0.15%)

Net exports = -0.46% (0.00%)

Boring Company CEO Steve Davis says he'll retire "the day I can commute from D.C. to Vegas in half an hour."

That would mean traveling more than 4,000 miles an hour. But before it can build a hyperloop, the Boring Company has to make tunnels cheap.

Since its founding in 2017, the company has brought tunneling costs below $10 million a mile. Davis expects that to fall to $4 million to $5 million, less than adding a lane to many urban highways.

"If we're below $5 million," Davis asks, "why would you ever build a road again?"

The most important consequence of this underground future may be the cost to access a city.

If a two-hour commute drops to ten minutes, inexpensive land far from the city could become a practical place to build homes. Eventually, tunnels could connect cities too.

"You can solve the rent and cost of living problem by making all of these places very desirable to live with just transportation," Davis says.

Stablecoin holders are giving up about ~$12B a year in T-bill income . That income goes to the issuers.

There should be a switch into these products but the data doesn't show it happening. Since the August peak stablecoins are down $17B and tokenised money market funds are down $2B as well, so money is leaving crypto rather than rotating into yield.

Part of the reason is these funds sit underneath stablecoins as much as beside them. Ethena's USDtb is ~99% backed by BlackRock's BUIDL and its supply has fallen from $877M at the end of Jan to about $350M. When stablecoins shrink, the funds backing them shrink too.

They're also mostly parked. Turnover is under 1x a month, so the back and forth that makes them interesting for a corporate treasury is still more promise than practice.

Until access opens up they're mainly plumbing for stablecoin issuers & trading firms, not yet an alternative for the treasurer sitting on idle stablecoins.

In TradFi, money market funds are an $8T market. Onchain the yield-paying version is $16.6B, 0.2% of that, against $287B of stablecoins paying their holders nothing. Cash naturally drifts to where it earns the bill rate, so that ratio should be multiples higher. That it isn't reflects a market structure that hasn't matured yet (access, plumbing, issuer incentives), and once it does I think these funds end up in the trillions.
